items.prompt: Which cloud service model gives the customer virtual machines, storage and networks to configure, while the provider manages the physical hardware?

options.label: FaaS
SaaS
IaaS
PaaS

rubric: IaaS provides raw virtualized infrastructure.
PaaS and SaaS hide more of the stack from the customer.

items.prompt: What term describes the ability of a cloud service to add or remove resources automatically as demand changes?

options.label: Encryption
Federation
Redundancy
Elasticity

rubric: Elasticity is automatic scaling with demand.
Redundancy is about duplication for availability, not scaling.

items.prompt: Which software layer lets one physical server run several isolated virtual machines?

options.label: Load balancer
Compiler
Firewall
Hypervisor

rubric: A hypervisor creates and manages VMs on shared hardware.
A load balancer distributes traffic, it does not virtualize hardware.

items.prompt: Which deployment model is cloud infrastructure shared by the general public and owned by a provider such as AWS or Azure?

options.label: Hybrid cloud
Public cloud
Community cloud
Private cloud

rubric: Public cloud is offered to many customers by a provider.
Private cloud is dedicated to a single organization.

items.prompt: What does the pay-as-you-go pricing model charge for?

options.label: A fixed yearly licence
Hardware purchase cost
Only the peak capacity ever reserved
Resources actually consumed

rubric: Pay-as-you-go bills for usage.
Fixed licences and hardware purchases are traditional models.

items.prompt: Which of the following are commonly recognized cloud deployment models? Select all that apply.

options.label: Private cloud
Public cloud
Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS)
Software as a Service (SaaS)

items.prompt: A small company wants to use email and calendar software delivered through a web browser. The provider handles servers, updates and the application itself. The company only manages its user accounts. Which service model is this?

options.label: On-premises hosting
PaaS
IaaS
SaaS

rubric: Complete applications delivered over the web are SaaS.
IaaS and PaaS require the customer to manage more, such as VMs or app code.

items.prompt: Why does virtualization help cloud providers lower costs?

options.label: Many customers' VMs share one server, raising hardware use
Each customer's workload gets its own dedicated physical server, which avoids resource contention between tenants
It makes networks faster by letting VMs skip the host operating system and talk to hardware directly
It removes the need for any physical data centers

rubric: Virtualization lets hardware be shared, improving utilization.
Dedicated servers and no data centers misdescribe how it works.

items.prompt: Under the shared responsibility model for IaaS, who is typically responsible for patching the guest operating system on a VM?

options.label: The hypervisor vendor
The customer
The provider
The internet service provider

rubric: In IaaS customers manage guest OS and above.
The provider secures the physical and virtualization layers.

items.prompt: How does PaaS differ from IaaS?

options.label: PaaS requires customers to build their own data centers
PaaS manages the OS and runtime; developers deploy code
PaaS gives raw hardware that customers must patch themselves
PaaS delivers finished end-user applications such as email

rubric: PaaS abstracts OS and runtime for developers.
Finished applications describe SaaS; raw machines describe IaaS.

items.prompt: A shop's website gets ten times more visitors on Black Friday only. Why is cloud elasticity useful here?

options.label: Traffic is spread out so fewer servers are needed overall
Capacity grows for the peak and shrinks after, so you pay less
Extra visitors are queued until the shop's fixed servers are free
Capacity is bought permanently for the peak, which guarantees speed

rubric: Elasticity matches capacity to temporary demand.
Permanent peak capacity wastes money.

items.prompt: Which describes a hybrid cloud?

options.label: Running every workload on one public cloud provider's VMs
Using two separate public SaaS products from different vendors
Hosting all servers in a company's own data center only
Combining private infrastructure with public cloud services

rubric: Hybrid combines private and public environments.
Using one public provider, several SaaS apps, or only an in-house data center is not hybrid.

items.prompt: Which statements correctly explain benefits of cloud computing compared with buying own servers? Select all that apply.

options.label: Resources can be provisioned in minutes
No large upfront hardware purchase is needed
The customer is responsible for the provider's physical security
Costs follow actual usage

rubric: Low upfront cost, fast provisioning and usage-based billing are cloud benefits.
Physical security belongs to the provider.

items.prompt: A startup stores customer files in a cloud object storage service. A data breach occurs because a bucket was set to public access by an employee. The startup blames the provider. Under the shared responsibility model, who is mainly responsible for this misconfiguration?

options.label: The provider, because it owns all the hardware
The startup, because customers configure access to their own data
The provider, because storage services are always secured for you
Nobody, because public buckets are a default law

rubric: Customers manage access settings and data in the cloud.
Provider responsibility covers the underlying infrastructure, not customer configuration.

items.prompt: A team tracks its projects in a hosted tool opened in a web browser. The vendor runs everything underneath, and the team only manages user accounts and its own project data. Which service model is this?

options.label: SaaS
IaaS
FaaS
PaaS

rubric: The customer consumes a finished application, which is SaaS.
PaaS and IaaS are chosen by learners who confuse using an app with building or hosting one.

items.prompt: Which statement best describes elasticity in cloud computing?

options.label: Data is copied to a second region so the service survives an outage
Servers are bought in advance so there is always spare room for peaks
Resources are added and removed automatically as demand rises and falls
Capacity is reserved for a year in return for a lower hourly rate

rubric: Elasticity means capacity follows demand, up and down.
Distractors describe over-provisioning, redundancy and commitment discounts, which are different ideas.

items.prompt: What is the main job of a hypervisor in a virtualized cloud host?

options.label: It copies each virtual machine to another server so that backups exist
It encrypts all network traffic that enters the data centre from the internet
It balances incoming requests evenly across a group of web servers
It lets several isolated virtual machines share one server's hardware

rubric: A hypervisor partitions physical hardware into isolated VMs.
Distractors confuse it with a firewall, a backup tool or a load balancer.

items.prompt: A company keeps its payroll system in its own data centre and runs its public website on a public cloud, linking the two. What is this deployment model called?

options.label: Community cloud
Public cloud
Private cloud
Hybrid cloud

rubric: Combining on-premises or private resources with public cloud is hybrid.
Public or private alone ignore the mix of environments.

items.prompt: Why does pay-as-you-go pricing suit a workload that is busy for only a few hours each week?

options.label: Rates drop automatically for the customer whenever the servers are idle
The provider gives a fixed discount on every resource regardless of usage
You pay once up front and then run the workload for free indefinitely
You are billed for the capacity used, so idle time costs little or nothing

rubric: Metered billing means unused time is not paid for.
Distractors invent flat discounts, one-time payments or automatic idle rate cuts.

items.prompt: Which of the following are widely accepted essential characteristics of cloud computing? Select all that apply.

options.label: Manual provisioning only through a support ticket
Customer-owned hardware installed on the customer's premises
Broad network access over standard networks
Measured service, with usage metered and billed
On-demand self-service provisioning

rubric: On-demand self-service, measured service and broad network access are core characteristics.
Customer-owned hardware and ticket-only provisioning describe traditional IT.

items.prompt: A company runs its web server on a rented virtual machine from an IaaS provider. An attacker exploits a known flaw in the operating system installed on that VM. Under the shared responsibility model, who was responsible for patching that guest operating system?

options.label: Both equally, because the shared model splits every task exactly in half
The provider, because every security patch in the cloud is applied by it
The provider, because it owns and operates the physical servers and hypervisor that the VM runs on
The customer, because the guest OS on an IaaS VM is the customer's to maintain

rubric: In IaaS the provider secures the infrastructure; the customer manages the guest OS and above.
Distractors assume the provider handles everything or that duties are split 50/50.

items.prompt: A VM costs 0.10 dollars per hour on demand and is billed only while running. A developer runs it 8 hours a day for 30 days and stops it each evening, with no other charges. What is the compute cost?

options.label: 24 dollars
240 dollars
8 dollars
72 dollars

rubric: 0.10 x 8 x 30 = 24 dollars.
72 assumes 24 hours a day; the others come from misplaced multiplication.

items.prompt: A small business needs to publish a static brochure website of HTML and images. Traffic is low and unpredictable, and they want almost no server administration. Which choice fits best?

options.label: Build a Kubernetes cluster across several availability zones
Rent a large VM and install a web server and operating system updates
Host the files in cloud object storage with static website hosting
Buy physical servers and place them in a rented rack

rubric: Object storage static hosting needs no servers to manage and costs little at low traffic.
The other options add administration and cost the workload does not need.

items.prompt: A team uses a managed PaaS database in which the provider patches the engine and runs backups. Which task still remains the team's responsibility?

options.label: Patching the database engine software when new versions appear
Replacing failed disks in the provider's data centre
Maintaining the hypervisor that hosts the database servers
Deciding who can connect and managing the database credentials

rubric: Access control and credentials stay with the customer even on managed services.
The other tasks are handled by the provider in a managed PaaS.

items.prompt: An online shop sees traffic jump tenfold for two hours every lunchtime and is quiet otherwise. Which design applies elasticity best?

options.label: A single very large server that handles lunchtime and idles otherwise
An auto scaling group that adds and removes web servers based on load
A fixed fleet sized for the lunchtime peak and kept running all day
A fixed small fleet that lunchtime customers must queue to use

rubric: Auto scaling matches capacity to the short peak and releases it afterwards.
Fixed fleets either waste money at idle or fail at peak.

items.prompt: A hospital must keep patient records on servers it owns, by policy, but wants to run its public appointment website in the cloud. Which deployment approach applies?

options.label: Community cloud shared with other unrelated businesses
Private on-premises only, with the website also kept in-house
Public cloud only, with records moved to the provider
Hybrid: records on premises, website on a public cloud

rubric: Hybrid keeps regulated data in-house while using public cloud for the website.
Other options ignore either the policy or the wish to use the cloud.

items.prompt: A development VM is used only on weekdays from 9 to 5. Its earlier test VMs were deleted but left their disks unattached and still billed. Which actions would reduce monthly cost? Select all that apply.

options.label: Delete the unattached disks left behind by the earlier test VMs
Move to a smaller instance size if CPU use stays low
Stop the VM automatically outside working hours
Add a second identical VM as a standby that stays on
Buy a three-year reserved commitment for always-on use

rubric: Scheduling, rightsizing and removing unused disks all cut billed resources.
A long always-on commitment or an extra VM increases cost for an intermittent workload.

items.prompt: A team must run a legacy application that needs a custom kernel module and a specific operating system version. They want to move it to the cloud without rewriting it. Which service model should they choose?

options.label: IaaS, because the team manages the guest OS on rented virtual machines
SaaS, because the vendor delivers the application ready to use today
PaaS, because the platform patches and runs the OS and runtime for them
Serverless functions, because the provider scales and runs the code on demand

rubric: Only IaaS gives control of the operating system and kernel.
PaaS, SaaS and serverless restrict OS-level changes, which the legacy app requires.

items.prompt: A team runs a web app on virtual machines. Traffic triples every weekday at 9 a.m. and drops by evening. They want capacity to match demand without manual action. Which setup do they apply?

options.label: A fixed fleet of VMs sized for the weekday peak and left running around the clock
A larger single VM that an engineer resizes by hand each morning and each evening before and after the traffic peak
An auto scaling group with a scale-out rule on average CPU and a scale-in rule for quiet periods
A second region holding an idle copy of the whole fleet, ready to take over if the first region fails

rubric: Auto scaling adds and removes instances automatically with demand, which is elasticity.
Peak-sized fixed fleets and manual resizing are not automatic; a second region addresses availability, not demand.

items.prompt: A startup wants to deploy a Python API and does not want to patch operating systems or manage web server software, but wants to control its own code and configuration. Which service model fits?

options.label: Bare-metal colocation, where the team owns the hardware and the provider supplies rack space
PaaS, where the provider manages the runtime and OS while the team deploys code
SaaS, where the team configures a finished vendor application and uploads its code
IaaS, where the team installs the runtime on rented VMs and patches the OS itself

rubric: PaaS removes OS and runtime management while keeping app code under the team's control.
IaaS leaves OS patching with the customer; SaaS does not host custom code.

items.prompt: A company runs a VM on IaaS. Under the shared responsibility model, which task falls to the company rather than the provider?

options.label: Applying security patches to the guest operating system
Replacing failed disks and storage arrays in the host servers
Patching and maintaining the hypervisor software on the hosts
Controlling physical access to the data center buildings

rubric: In IaaS the customer owns the guest OS and everything above it.
The other tasks are provider duties for physical and virtualization layers.

items.prompt: A VM costs 0.10 per hour on demand. A batch job needs 200 VM-hours and runs once a month. A reserved one-year commitment for the same VM costs 0.06 per hour for all 8,760 hours. Which is cheaper for this job, per year?

options.label: They cost the same because the compute used is identical
On demand: about 240 total versus about 525 reserved
Reserved, because the hourly rate is lower in every case
Reserved: about 240 total versus about 525 on demand

rubric: On demand: 200 x 12 x 0.10 = 240; reserved: 8,760 x 0.06 is about 525.
Reserved rates are billed for every hour, so low usage makes them wasteful.

items.prompt: A host has 32 GB of RAM and runs a hypervisor. A team wants to place VMs of 6 GB each, ignoring hypervisor overhead and overcommit. How many such VMs fit?
rubric: 32 / 6 is 5.33, so only 5 whole VMs fit.
Rounding up to 6 ignores that a VM cannot be partially placed.

items.prompt: A team must keep a customer-facing service running if one availability zone fails. Which actions apply this goal? Select all that apply.

options.label: Store all data on a single instance's local disk
Put all instances in one zone with larger instance sizes
Spread instances across at least two availability zones
Place a load balancer in front of instances in different zones

rubric: Multi-zone placement plus load balancing lets traffic survive one zone failing.
Bigger instances in one zone and single local disks keep a single point of failure.

items.prompt: A small firm needs email, calendar and document editing for 40 staff. It has no administrators and wants no servers to maintain, paying per user monthly. A consultant suggests a service model. Which model should the firm apply?

options.label: PaaS, writing a custom mail app on a managed runtime
A private cloud built in the firm's office
SaaS, using a hosted productivity suite billed per user
IaaS, building a mail server on rented VMs

rubric: SaaS delivers finished applications with per-user billing and no servers to run.
IaaS, PaaS and private cloud all need technical staff the firm lacks.

items.prompt: A web tier autoscales on CPU, but during a sale response times climb while CPU stays at 25%. Instances are waiting on a single database connection limit. What is the most likely cause?

options.label: The VMs are too small, so they cannot use their available CPU
A shared downstream limit is the bottleneck, so more web instances won't help
The load balancer is using the wrong protocol, so requests queue before reaching the web tier
The autoscaling policy is scaling in too fast, so too few instances remain to serve the sale traffic

rubric: Low CPU with high latency and waiting on connections points to a shared downstream limit.
Scaling policy or VM size would show up as high CPU or instance count changes.

items.prompt: A monthly bill rose 40% though traffic was flat. Compute hours are unchanged, but data transfer out to the internet and cross-region replication charges both grew. Which analysis fits?

options.label: Elasticity failed to scale in, so review autoscaling policies and idle instance time
Compute rates rose, so rightsizing instances or buying reserved capacity will fix it
Data movement charges rose, so review where data is read from and replicated to
Storage tiers changed, so move older objects to a cheaper class to cut the bill

rubric: Unchanged compute with higher transfer and replication points to egress and replication costs.
The other options contradict the stated unchanged compute or invent causes.

items.prompt: A company stores sensitive files in an object bucket, and a breach exposed them. The bucket policy allowed public read. The provider's data centers were not compromised. Who is responsible for the misconfiguration?

options.label: The provider, because public read is on by default in all services
The customer, because access settings on its own data are its duty
The provider, because it hosts the storage service
Both equally, because the bucket runs on shared hardware

rubric: Customers configure access to their data even on managed services.
Hosting or shared hardware does not move configuration duty to the provider.

items.prompt: A team compares moving an app to IaaS VMs versus PaaS. The app needs a custom kernel module. Which factor most decides against PaaS?

options.label: PaaS runs on shared hardware, so tenants cannot isolate workloads
PaaS restricts OS-level access, so the module can't be loaded
PaaS bills per request, so a kernel module would cost too much
PaaS cannot scale instances, so the module would not keep up

rubric: Managed runtimes hide the OS, so kernel-level changes need IaaS.
PaaS does scale and runs on shared hardware; the other claims are not general.

items.prompt: A noisy VM on a shared host slows other tenants' VMs in disk performance even though each has its own virtual disk. Which part of virtualization explains this?

options.label: Each virtual disk is backed by a dedicated physical disk, so contention cannot occur
The hypervisor lets the busy VM borrow other VMs' virtual disks when idle
Virtual network isolation also throttles disk access between tenants on one host
Virtual disks map onto shared physical storage whose I/O is split among tenants

rubric: Isolation is logical; underlying physical I/O is shared and can contend.
Dedicated disks per VM would eliminate the effect; memory copying is not how hypervisors work.

items.prompt: An app on autoscaled VMs loses user sessions at random after scale-in events. Which causes could explain this? Select all that apply.

options.label: The load balancer sends users to different instances without shared session storage
The VMs use a virtualized network
The cloud provider bills per hour
Sessions are held in each instance's local memory

rubric: Local session state is lost when instances are removed or users are routed elsewhere.
Virtual networking and billing do not cause session loss.

items.prompt: A firm keeps customer records on premises for legal reasons but runs its public website in a public cloud, with the site calling an internal API over a VPN. Pages are slow whenever the API is queried. Which analysis best isolates the cause of the slowness?

options.label: Disable the VPN for a day, since encryption overhead is the most likely source of the delay
Move the website to a larger VM, since the cloud web tier is probably underpowered under load
Measure latency and bandwidth on the VPN link, since each page waits on cross-boundary calls
Replace the public cloud with SaaS, since hybrid designs add delay that cannot be tuned out

rubric: In a hybrid design, calls across the link add latency, so measuring it targets the likely cause.
Resizing or abandoning hybrid guesses at causes without evidence.

items.prompt: An autoscaling group adds an instance when average CPU exceeds 70% and removes one when it drops below 65%. New instances need about 5 minutes to become ready. Under steady load, capacity keeps growing and shrinking every few minutes. What best explains this?

options.label: The 5-minute boot time means new instances are billed twice, which forces the group to shrink right after growing
The two thresholds are close and there is no cooldown, so each action pushes CPU across the opposite threshold
The provider throttles scaling API calls, so decisions arrive late and are applied out of order each time
Scaling in is always slower than scaling out, so the group overshoots capacity before it settles down

rubric: A narrow gap between thresholds with no cooldown causes flapping: each scale action moves the metric across the other trigger.
Distractors blame provider throttling, scale-in speed or billing, none of which produce repeated oscillation.

items.prompt: A team stores customer files in a provider-managed object storage service. A breach occurs because a bucket was set to public read. The provider's hardware and service software were fully patched. Which analysis is most accurate?

options.label: The customer's access configuration failed; the provider secures the service, but customers control who can reach their data
Patching was insufficient because public exposure is usually caused by a hypervisor flaw in the storage layer
The provider is at fault because managed services take over responsibility for access settings along with the infrastructure
The failure is shared equally because all data on provider hardware is jointly owned and jointly protected by both sides

rubric: Under shared responsibility, customers own data and access configuration even on managed services.
Distractors assume managed means fully outsourced security or blame infrastructure.

items.prompt: A web app in region A queries a database in region B. Compute and storage unit prices are normal, yet the bill is high and page latency is poor. Which is the most likely common cause?

options.label: Storage in region B is always billed at a premium rate regardless of how much data is actually used
Virtualization overhead grows whenever two regions are linked, which inflates the CPU charges on both sides
Idle instances in region A are billed at triple rate whenever they make remote calls to another region
Cross-region data transfer adds per-GB charges and extra round-trip time on every query the app makes

rubric: Inter-region traffic is billed per GB and adds network latency; co-locating app and data removes both.
Distractors invent pricing rules that do not exist.

items.prompt: After placing a web app behind a load balancer with four instances, users are randomly logged out. Each instance keeps session data in its own memory. What is the root cause?

options.label: A user's requests reach different instances and only one holds that session, so state is not shared
Four instances exceed the number of concurrent sessions that the cloud provider allows for one application
Horizontal scaling resets each instance clock, so session timestamps expire early on the other nodes
The load balancer encrypts cookies with a different key on every request, which invalidates the sessions

rubric: Local in-memory session state breaks under horizontal scaling; use shared session storage or stickiness.
Distractors invent load balancer or provider behaviours.

items.prompt: A VM on a shared multi-tenant host shows average CPU of 30%, but p99 request latency spikes at irregular times and the guest OS reports high CPU steal time. Which diagnosis fits best?

options.label: The VM is oversized, so the hypervisor keeps spending time reclaiming vCPUs that the guest is not using
The guest OS has a memory leak, which the kernel reports as steal time in its CPU statistics output
The network between availability zones is saturated, which the guest reports as CPU steal time on its vCPUs
Other tenants on the same host are competing for physical CPU, so the hypervisor delays this VM's scheduling

rubric: Steal time means the hypervisor ran something else while the guest wanted CPU: a noisy neighbour on shared hardware.
Distractors attribute steal time to memory, networking or VM size.

items.prompt: A team lifts and shifts an on-prem VM estate to IaaS, and the monthly bill exceeds the on-prem estimate. Which factors plausibly explain this? Select all that apply.

options.label: Data leaving the provider network to users or other networks is charged per GB
Per-core software licences may cost more on certain provider instance types
VMs sized for on-prem peak run 24/7 at on-demand rates, so idle capacity is billed
Shared responsibility moves hardware maintenance costs back onto the customer
Providers add a surcharge for each virtualization layer used beyond the first one

rubric: Idle oversized capacity, egress fees and licensing are common causes of lift-and-shift cost overruns.
Virtualization surcharges and customer hardware costs do not exist; the provider maintains hardware.

items.prompt: A team replaced a VM running a steadily busy API (about 400 requests per second around the clock) with functions billed per invocation and duration. The monthly bill rose sharply and some first requests are slow. Which analysis best explains the result?

options.label: Per-use pricing suits spiky load; at constant high load it costs more than an always-on VM, and cold starts slow first requests
Functions cannot scale beyond a single instance, so the extra cost comes from retries piling up on one overloaded worker process
Serverless platforms bill for idle time between invocations, and that idle charge dominates total cost once request rates are high
Slow first requests show the functions share hardware with other tenants, and that shared hosting also raises their unit prices

rubric: Pay-per-use beats provisioned capacity at low utilisation but loses at sustained high utilisation; cold starts explain slow first calls.
Distractors misstate scaling and billing of functions.

items.prompt: A firm must keep customer records in its own data centre for regulatory reasons. Its analytics jobs need ten times normal capacity for two days each month. Criteria: records stay on-prem, and no idle hardware is bought for the peak. Which approach fits best?

options.label: Community cloud: share the on-prem hardware with other firms in the sector to cover the two-day monthly peak
Public cloud only: move everything, since elasticity removes any need for on-prem systems and satisfies the regulator
Hybrid: records stay on-prem, and peak analytics run on public cloud using only data the regulation allows to leave
Private cloud only: buy hardware for the monthly peak so that all data and compute stay in-house at all times

rubric: Hybrid meets both criteria: regulated data stays put and burst capacity is rented only when needed.
Distractors either ignore the regulation or buy idle peak hardware.

items.prompt: A service has a steady baseline of 20 instances all year and unpredictable spikes up to 60 instances. Criteria: minimise cost and never run short of capacity during spikes. Which purchasing plan is best?

options.label: Reserve capacity for the 20 baseline instances and autoscale on-demand instances for the spikes
Use on-demand for all instances, since unpredictable spikes make a commitment on the steady baseline too risky to be worthwhile
Reserve 60 instances for a year so spike capacity is guaranteed and every instance gets a discounted hourly rate
Run all 60 instances on spot capacity, since it has the lowest hourly price and most spikes are short enough to ride out

rubric: Commitments discount the predictable baseline; on-demand covers the variable part without paying for idle reservations.
Distractors over-reserve, risk spot interruption, or forgo discounts on a known baseline.

items.prompt: Spot instances are cheap but can be reclaimed with a two-minute warning. Criterion: minimise cost without harming availability or correctness. Which workload is the best fit?

options.label: A real-time API gateway with strict latency targets and no spare capacity held in reserve
The primary node of a transactional database that serves live customer orders around the clock
A stateless video-transcoding batch that checkpoints progress and can resume on any node
A single-instance licence server that every client application contacts continuously during work hours

rubric: Interruption-tolerant, restartable batch work gains savings without risk.
The other options are stateful or single points of failure that interruptions would harm.

items.prompt: A three-person team must launch a standard web app. Criteria: minimal OS patching and server management, ability to deploy their own code, no custom runtimes needed. Which service model fits best?

options.label: Colocated bare-metal servers, because full hardware control suits the app and management can be scripted over time
IaaS, because virtual machines give the most control and the team can automate patching themselves later
PaaS, because the provider manages OS and runtime while the team deploys its own code on the platform
SaaS, because a vendor-run application removes all operations work even though the team cannot deploy its own code

rubric: PaaS removes OS and runtime upkeep while still letting the team run its own code.
IaaS leaves patching to the team; SaaS does not allow custom code.

items.prompt: An online store must survive the loss of a single data centre with recovery under 5 minutes, on a tight budget. There is no regulatory need for geographic separation. Which design best meets these criteria?

options.label: Active-active across two regions, since only separate regions can protect against a data centre failure
A single availability zone with nightly backups restored onto a new instance after any failure occurs
Several availability zones in one region with automatic failover and a load balancer in front
A single availability zone with a larger instance type, since bigger instances fail much less often

rubric: Multi-AZ covers a data centre loss with fast failover at far lower cost than multi-region.
Distractors overspend, rely on slow restores, or misjudge instance size as resilience.

items.prompt: A small team proposes running identical active-active stacks on two cloud providers purely for resilience. Which are valid criticisms of this plan? Select all that apply.

options.label: Shared responsibility rules prohibit one application from running on more than one provider
The team must master two sets of services and tooling, which raises operational risk
Cross-provider traffic adds egress charges and latency for any synchronous data replication
Using only features common to both providers gives up the managed services that deliver most benefits
Each provider's SLA is void when another provider hosts part of the same application

rubric: Complexity, lowest-common-denominator design and egress/latency costs are real multi-cloud trade-offs.
No rule bars multi-provider use, and SLAs are not voided by it.

items.prompt: A two-person startup needs a relational database with point-in-time recovery and automated failover. Neither person is a DBA, and they rank low operational burden above full control. They worry about lock-in, but the app uses standard PostgreSQL features only. Which choice best fits?

options.label: A managed PostgreSQL service, since it handles recovery and failover while standard SQL keeps migration cost low
PostgreSQL on self-managed VMs, since full control avoids lock-in and they can script backups and failover
A proprietary managed NoSQL database, since it has the strongest automation and lock-in matters little to them
A single VM database with nightly snapshots, since it is simplest and recovery within hours is acceptable

rubric: A managed service meets the ops-burden and recovery criteria, and standard PostgreSQL limits lock-in.
Self-managing needs DBA skills; the other options fail the recovery or compatibility criteria.

items.prompt: A team must pick a model for a steady, predictable workload that runs 24/7 at about 80% of provisioned capacity for three years. Criteria: lowest total cost, no need for burst capacity, tolerance for commitment. Which pricing approach best fits?

options.label: Serverless functions, because per-invocation billing avoids paying for idle time and stays cheapest when utilization is constant and high for years
Spot instances for the nodes, because the deepest discount outweighs interruption risk when the service is built to tolerate restarts
Committed-use or reserved capacity, because a steady known load earns a discount that on-demand rates cannot match
On-demand instances, because per-second billing with no commitment keeps cost lowest and preserves flexibility if needs change later

rubric: Steady, predictable load is the case where commitments beat on-demand pricing.
Distractors assume pay-per-use or interruptible capacity is always cheapest, ignoring utilization.

items.prompt: A company evaluates moving a stateful, licensed legacy app unchanged to the cloud. Criteria: minimal code change, full OS-level control for the vendor agent, fast migration. Which service model is the best trade-off?

options.label: SaaS replacement, because the vendor manages everything and preserves the current custom agent unchanged
PaaS app platform, because managed runtimes remove OS work and accept unmodified legacy apps without changes
IaaS virtual machines, because they give OS control and allow lift-and-shift without rewriting the app
Function-as-a-service, because stateless handlers run any legacy binary with no refactoring or state handling

rubric: Lift-and-shift with OS control points to IaaS.
PaaS and FaaS impose runtime and statelessness constraints; SaaS removes control.

items.prompt: A regulated bank wants to keep customer records on its own hardware for legal reasons but needs extra compute for month-end analytics. Criteria: data residency, cost of peak capacity, minimal duplicate infrastructure. Which deployment judgement is best?

options.label: Public cloud only, because providers' compliance certifications automatically transfer legal liability for the records
Multi-cloud across two providers, because spreading records across vendors satisfies residency requirements by itself
Private cloud only, because sizing it for month-end peak is cheaper than renting elastic capacity occasionally
Hybrid cloud: keep records on-premises and burst anonymised analytics workloads to public cloud at peaks

rubric: Hybrid satisfies residency while using elasticity for peaks.
Distractors misread compliance transfer, peak economics, or what multi-cloud solves.

items.prompt: A startup's engineer claims: 'We use a managed database service, so the provider is responsible for our data being secure.' Which critique is most accurate under shared responsibility?

options.label: Fully correct: the provider takes over identity policies, network exposure rules and data protection once the database is managed
Mostly correct: the provider secures the engine and hosts, and the customer only needs to supply encryption keys when asked
Wrong: managed services shift little, so the customer must still patch the database engine and the underlying hosts
Partly wrong: the provider secures the infrastructure and engine, but the customer owns access control, configuration and data

rubric: Customers always keep identity, configuration and data responsibility.
Distractors overstate or deny the transfer of responsibility.

items.prompt: Two designs serve a web app with traffic that spikes 20x for ten minutes unpredictably. A: autoscaling VM group with 3-minute boot time. B: containers on a managed platform scaling in seconds with a small warm pool. Criteria: protect user latency during spikes, moderate cost. Which is the better judgement?

options.label: B, because containers remove capacity limits entirely, so cost stays flat however large the spike becomes
A, because full VMs isolate each workload better, so they absorb a sudden spike with less latency risk
A, because autoscaling policies add VMs as load rises, so users see no delay even while new VMs boot
B, because fast scale-out plus a warm pool covers the spike while VMs would still be booting

rubric: Scale-out latency versus spike duration decides; fast scaling protects latency.
Distractors misstate boot behavior or claim costs vanish.

items.prompt: A team judges a proposal to run a batch job on spot/preemptible instances. Which criteria-based observations are sound? Select all that apply.

options.label: Cost savings can be large, but capacity may be reclaimed on short notice
It suits a latency-sensitive primary database needing continuous uptime
It suits jobs that checkpoint progress and tolerate interruption
Spot capacity carries a guaranteed availability SLA for long jobs

rubric: Spot pairs with interruption-tolerant work and trades reliability for price.
Distractors assume continuous uptime or an availability guarantee.

items.prompt: A media firm's render farm needs 500 cores for 6 hours twice a month. An architect proposes buying servers; another proposes IaaS on demand. Cost of owned hardware is fixed whatever the usage; cloud costs only when running. Which judgement is best?

options.label: Reserve 500 cores for three years, because committed-use discounts beat on-demand pricing even at under 2% utilization
Use on-demand or spot cloud capacity, because utilization is very low and elasticity avoids paying for idle hardware
Buy servers, because owning hardware is always cheaper than any rental once the purchase price is amortized over years
Buy servers, because cloud cores run slower than physical ones so the jobs would exceed the six-hour window each time

rubric: Low, bursty utilization favors pay-per-use elasticity.
Distractors ignore utilization or misapply commitments.

items.prompt: Design requirement: a web tier must survive loss of an entire datacenter, scale with load, and not lose user sessions. Which design meets all three?

options.label: Two zones with fixed instance counts and sticky sessions on local disk, so each user stays pinned to one server
Stateless instances in an autoscaling group across multiple zones, with sessions in a replicated external store
One large VM in a single zone with a nightly snapshot, since a bigger instance handles load and snapshots protect sessions
Autoscaling instances in one zone holding sessions in local memory, relying on the load balancer to recover from a zone failure

rubric: Multi-AZ, elastic, stateless tier with externalized sessions meets all constraints.
Distractors fail on zone loss, session durability, or elasticity.

items.prompt: You must design file ingestion: unpredictable uploads, processing takes 1-5 minutes each, no idle cost, and a failed job must be retried without losing the upload. Which design fits every constraint?

options.label: A single always-on VM polls a folder every minute and processes files serially, restarting itself after failure
Uploads to object storage trigger a queue message; autoscaled workers consume it and retry failed messages
A cron job on a fixed cluster scans storage hourly and reprocesses everything each run, avoiding any lost uploads
A synchronous web request processes each upload in the API server, returning when done so failures are visible

rubric: Event plus queue plus scaled workers gives zero idle cost and retries.
Others incur idle cost, tie up request threads, or reprocess wastefully.

items.prompt: Design a multi-tenant SaaS: each customer's data must be isolated, onboarding must be automated, and cost per small tenant must stay low. Which design best meets all?

options.label: A separate cloud account per tenant with hand-built networks, because accounts cost nothing to manage at scale
One shared database table with no tenant identifier, relying on the application UI to hide other customers' rows
A dedicated VM and database per tenant created manually by an operator, giving strongest isolation for everyone
Shared compute with tenant-scoped identity and per-tenant data partitions, provisioned by automated templates

rubric: Shared compute with scoped partitions and automation balances isolation and cost.
Distractors break automation, isolation, or cost.

items.prompt: A design must recover from a regional outage within 15 minutes with at most 1 minute of data loss, at the lowest cost that meets it. Which plan fits?

options.label: Single-region multi-zone deployment with hourly snapshots, since zones protect against regional outages
Asynchronously replicate data to a second region and keep a scaled-down warm standby that scales up on failover
Daily backups copied to a second region, rebuilt from scratch on failure using infrastructure templates
Full active-active in three regions with synchronous writes everywhere, regardless of cost or write latency

rubric: Warm standby with continuous replication meets RTO/RPO cheaply.
Others miss RPO/RTO, overspend, or misunderstand zone scope.

items.prompt: You must reduce vendor lock-in risk for a containerized app while keeping operations small. Which plan best meets both constraints?

options.label: Package in standard containers with infrastructure-as-code, using managed services behind thin interfaces where portability matters
Run every component on self-managed VMs to avoid any provider-specific service, accepting the large burden of patching, scaling and operating databases and queues yourself
Deploy simultaneously on three clouds, using each cloud's proprietary features, so any one provider can be dropped without changing application behavior
Adopt each provider's proprietary services deeply for speed, since lock-in disappears once contracts include exit clauses and data export rights

rubric: Standards plus abstraction limits lock-in without heavy ops.
Distractors inflate ops, ignore technical lock-in, or assume parity.

items.prompt: A proposed design for a public API uses one autoscaling VM group behind a load balancer, one database instance, and an admin port open to the internet. Which additions are needed to meet requirements of high availability and least-privilege security? Select all that apply.

options.label: Give each engineer the shared administrator account so access can be audited by team rather than by person
Move to a larger database instance size so the single database has enough capacity headroom to avoid outages
Restrict admin access to a private network or VPN with scoped roles
Database replica or failover in another zone

rubric: Redundancy removes the single DB point of failure; restricting admin access applies least privilege.
Bigger VMs do not give redundancy; shared credentials violate least privilege.

items.prompt: A retailer needs a checkout design: handle Black Friday 30x peaks, never charge a customer twice if a request is retried, and keep costs low off-peak. Which design satisfies every constraint?

options.label: Fixed fleet sized for 30x peak all year, with retries disabled so duplicate charges cannot occur
Autoscaled stateless services with idempotency keys on payment requests and a queue to smooth load to the database
A single large instance scaled up manually before the sale, with clients resubmitting the form upon any delay
Autoscaled services that retry payments automatically on timeout without keys, relying on the gateway to deduplicate

rubric: Elasticity plus idempotency keys covers peak, cost and duplicate protection.
Distractors waste cost, risk duplicates, or lack elasticity.
